1509e26669.q: What does Caroline Goldman say about timeouts as a parenting tool?
1509e26669.a: Goldman strongly promotes the timeout as a core disciplinary tool, arguing it gives children a clear signal about which boundary they have crossed and…
f: Caroline Goldman is a strong advocate for the timeout as a core disciplinary tool, arguing that it sends children a clear signal about which boundary they have crossed while allowing everyone involved to calm down. In her book Go to Your Room , she outlines a list of forbidden behaviors starting from age one and recommends timeouts of at least 30 minutes for children over the age of four — a duration that directly contradicts most established research on the subject, which calls for significantly shorter periods.

Goldman's position on timeouts sits at the heart of a fierce national debate in France between traditional disciplinary parenting and the newer "positive parenting" movement championed by figures like psychologist Isabelle Filliozat. For Goldman and her allies — who numbered over 350 early childhood experts when they signed an open letter in Le Figaro in 2022 — the problem with the gentle parenting wave is that it left children without the clear limits they need. The timeout, in her framework, is precisely that limit made concrete and felt.

The pushback was swift and organized. Some 280 early childhood experts signed a competing open letter in Le Monde specifically opposing the use of timeouts — an unusually direct rebuttal in French public intellectual life. The disagreement is not merely about duration; it reflects a deeper conflict about what children need from adults. You can follow the full exchange between these two camps in the episode on The Daily .

"Parents were essentially abandoned by adults with an exclusively empathic attitude — and for Goldman and her allies, that is exactly why it is time to go back to a more disciplinary form of education."
— Madeline Schwartz, reporter, The New York Times About Madeline Schwartz

MS Madeline Schwartz Reporter · The New York Times Madeline Schwartz is a reporter for The New York Times, based in Paris. She grew up between New York and Paris, attending school in both cities — the child of an American mother and a French father who separated when she was a baby.

6810d37e3b.q: What did the 2019 French Anti-Spanking Law change, and why is it controversial in the parenting debate?
6810d37e3b.a: France's 2019 law, known colloquially as the Anti-Spanking Law, forbids physical and psychological violence against children, including what it terms…
f: France's 2019 Anti-Spanking Law forbids both physical and psychological violence against children, including what it terms "ordinary educational violence." The law's critical flaw — and the source of ongoing controversy — is that it never defines what "ordinary educational violence" actually means, leaving parents, practitioners, and legal experts in a genuine grey zone.

That definitional gap has become a battlefield in the broader French parenting debate. Psychologist Caroline Goldman and her allies argue that practices like the timeout — sending a child to their room as a disciplinary measure — are entirely lawful and even beneficial. Goldman's book Go to Your Room explicitly recommends timeouts of at least 30 minutes for children over the age of four, framing them as a healthy, structured consequence that helps children understand which boundary they have crossed.

But a significant bloc of early childhood educators reads the law very differently. For them, timeouts fall squarely within the prohibited category of psychological violence — a position backed by the 280 experts who signed a competing open letter in Le Monde opposing the use of timeouts. The result is a situation where the same parenting tool is simultaneously defended as responsible discipline and condemned as a violation of the law — with no official clarification in sight. The full conversation behind this dispute is available on Listenly in the episode of The Daily .
Key term from the episode

"Ordinary educational violence" — the phrase used in France's 2019 Anti-Spanking Law to describe the category of behaviour it prohibits. The law bans it without ever specifying what acts fall under this label, which is precisely what makes it legally and philosophically ambiguous. Whether a timeout constitutes ordinary educational violence remains a live, unresolved question among French childcare professionals.

"Parents were essentially abandoned by adults with an exclusively empathic attitude — and for Goldman and her allies, that is exactly why it is time to go back to a more disciplinary form of education."

bccf3f936e.q: What are the key functions and data tracking capabilities of modern baby monitors like Nanit?
bccf3f936e.a: The Nanit is a baby monitor that hooks up to home Wi-Fi and lives as an app on a phone. The app tracks the baby's movements, logs when they woke up and fell asleep, can see when their eyes open and close, and puts all this information into a digestible format for parents showing how many times they visited overnight, hours of sleep, wake-ups, and duration before the baby put themselves back to sleep.
bccf3f936e.e: Health Trackers Are Everywhere. Do Babies Need Them, Too?
f: Nanit monitors record a continuous stream of sleep data —tracking when babies wake and fall asleep, how long they stay awake between visits, eye movements, and the frequency of nighttime check-ins by parents. The app transforms raw video footage into a digestible summary dashboard showing hours slept, wake-up counts, and self-soothing duration.

The appeal is clear: while a typical pediatric checkup lasts only 22 minutes and children visit the doctor once a year on average, Nanit delivers granular, real-time insights parents can review nightly. As Sapna Mashwari explores in The Daily , the monitor connects to your home Wi-Fi and operates entirely through a smartphone app, turning what was once a simple audio baby monitor into an AI-powered health surveillance device.

What makes Nanit distinctive among baby health trackers is its focus on behavioral patterns rather than vital signs. The system doesn't measure heart rate or oxygen levels—instead, it uses computer vision to analyze movement and rest cycles. This data-heavy approach appealed to Mashwari when her first child was born four years ago, though she admits the constant visibility felt unsettling at first.

Computer vision in baby monitors: The technology that powers Nanit analyzes video footage frame-by-frame to detect when a baby's eyes open or close, how much they move, and when they transition between sleep stages. The AI learns individual patterns over time, making the data increasingly personalized. The company itself has recognized the power of this early-stage data collection. Nanit raised $50 million last year and has positioned itself strategically in a booming market— as detailed in this episode , the broader wearables market is approaching $100 billion, and companies are racing to capture health tracking from birth onward. Nanit's leadership envisions capturing data from infancy through childhood, reasoning that since 90 percent of a child's brain develops between ages zero and five, early behavioral data could become invaluable.
"We envision a world where people will have their data from zero to 100, and right now people are starting to wear Apple watches around age 10, so we really think about zero to 10 as where we live."

Anushka Salinas — CEO, Nanit. Salinas leads the company's vision to establish continuous health data collection from infancy, positioning baby monitoring as the entry point to lifelong health tracking ecosystems.

82c936b2d5.q: How do health wearables like Whoop and Oura rings use AI to provide personalized health recommendations?
82c936b2d5.a: These devices track sleep, exercise habits, and provide recovery scores based on metrics like stress, illness, diet quality, and workout intensity. Whoop offers a recovery score in three colors—red, yellow, and green—that tells users how ready their body is to take on the day, though these are consumer products, not medical devices.
82c936b2d5.e: Health Trackers Are Everywhere. Do Babies Need Them, Too?
f: These devices analyze sleep quality, exercise patterns, and recovery metrics —including stress levels, illness indicators, diet, and workout intensity—then translate that data into actionable daily scores. Whoop uses a three-color system (red, yellow, green) to show your body's readiness, though it's important to remember these are consumer products, not medical devices.

The wearables market is approaching $100 billion according to analysts, with half of Americans already owning at least one health tracking device. Devices like Whoop, Oura rings, and smartwatches continuously gather biometric information and feed it through algorithms designed to spot patterns in your behavior and physiology.

As Sapna Mashwari explains in The Daily episode , these tools can offer real value for people serious about optimizing their health—but they also blur the line between helpful insight and anxiety-inducing data overload. The color-coded recovery score, for example, tells you whether you're physically prepared to handle training or exercise that day, reducing the guesswork around when to push hard versus when to rest.
The fine line between insight and consumer product

What makes these devices compelling is their personalized, real-time feedback based on your individual baseline. Rather than a generic fitness recommendation, Whoop learns how your body responds to stress, sleep deprivation, and exercise over time, then adapts its recommendations accordingly. This is where machine learning earns its place—the algorithm improves as it collects more data about you.

Yet the critical distinction remains: these are consumer wellness tools, not clinical instruments. They're built to motivate and inform, not to diagnose or treat medical conditions. The metrics they track—heart rate variability, skin temperature, movement patterns—are real and measurable, but the conclusions drawn from them exist in a zone of probabilistic guidance rather than medical certainty. Anyone relying on a wearable to make serious health decisions should still consult a healthcare provider.

c87f37177c.q: What geographic advantage allowed Saudi Arabia to maintain oil exports while the Strait of Hormuz was blockaded during the Iran war?
c87f37177c.a: Saudi Arabia had built a gigantic oil pipeline that stretches across the kingdom to the Red Sea, allowing them to export oil over land as a workaround when the Strait of Hormuz became choked off. This pipeline had been built as a precautionary measure and suddenly became critical when they needed an alternative route to get oil to their global customers.
c87f37177c.e: Why Gas Prices Just Keep Going Up
f: Saudi Arabia built a massive oil pipeline stretching across the kingdom to the Red Sea , which allowed them to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when it became blockaded. This pipeline had been constructed as a precautionary measure years earlier and suddenly became essential when the Iran conflict threatened their primary export route.

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints, responsible for moving vast quantities of oil to global markets. When regional tensions escalated and the strait faced potential blockade, this strategic vulnerability threatened Saudi Arabia's economic lifeline. However, the kingdom had planned ahead.

As Vivian Neerheim explains in The Daily episode , the East-West Pipeline provided an alternative route that fundamentally changed the equation. Rather than depending entirely on shipping through the contested strait, Saudi Arabia could move oil overland to Red Sea ports, then export to the rest of the world from there.

This infrastructure decision, made well before the crisis, transformed how the kingdom managed geopolitical risk. The pipeline became a practical hedge against blockade scenarios that many analysts thought were merely theoretical until the conflict actually unfolded.
"As long as there is still conflict in the region and as long as they have foes who are still willing and able to attack the pipeline, that will remain a risk."

f: In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea , then pushed toward the coast and seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait. On the same Friday they took this strategic territory, Saudi Arabia announced its crucial east-west pipeline had been attacked and had to be shut down, choking off nearly all remaining exits for Arabian Peninsula oil.

The sequence of events unfolded with striking timing. The Houthis' territorial gains positioned them to control one of the world's most critical shipping lanes, but the real shock came when the pipeline attack occurred on the same day—leaving Saudi Arabia without its backup route for exporting oil. As Vivian Neerheim explains in the episode , this double disruption created an unprecedented squeeze on global energy supplies.

The pipeline had served as Saudi Arabia's insurance policy after the Strait of Hormuz became a flashpoint during the Iran war. With both routes now compromised or closed , the kingdom's ability to move oil to international markets collapsed almost overnight. This wasn't a gradual market shift—it was a sudden, coordinated loss of export capacity that rippled immediately into gas prices at pumps across the United States, where consumers saw a 20-cent jump per gallon in a single 24-hour period .
"As long as there is still conflict in the region and as long as they have foes who are still willing and able to attack the pipeline, that will remain a risk."

f: Trump rejected military intervention against the Houthis for three core reasons: the Houthis have no desire to attack the United States directly, only Saudi Arabia ; the U.S. previously launched an airstrike campaign against them with poor results; and they have repeatedly forced far more powerful adversaries to concede defeat, making military engagement an unlikely path to victory.

The Trump administration's reluctance reflects a strategic calculation rooted in recent history. A previous U.S. airstrike campaign against the Houthis proved brief and ineffectual , yielding no lasting military advantage and suggesting that air power alone cannot resolve the conflict. This precedent weighs heavily on current decision-making.

More fundamentally, the Houthis have demonstrated an unusual capacity for resilience against overwhelming force. Despite facing adversaries with vastly superior resources and military capabilities, they have forced multiple foes to back down from sustained engagement. This pattern—repeated across years of regional conflict—suggests that traditional military solutions may not apply to this particular threat.

As detailed in The Daily's reporting from the region , the Houthis control the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea, a strategic chokepoint that gives them leverage far beyond what their economic or military resources would normally permit. Their threat to Saudi oil infrastructure stems not from technological superiority but from geography and will.

34addf4256.a: Saudi Arabia's options include going back to war with the Houthis to force them to back down militarily, which didn't go well the first time. Another option is to negotiate a diplomatic solution, but the Houthis have a history of maximalist demands and are unlikely to back down easily now that they feel they have the upper hand. f: Saudi Arabia faces two constrained paths forward: renew a costly military campaign against the Houthis that already failed once, or pursue diplomacy with an adversary known for maximalist demands and no guarantee of compliance. Neither option breaks the blockade with certainty.

The first option is military. A return to war with the Houthis means Saudi Arabia must force them to back down by combat—a strategy that has already been tried. Saudi Arabia's prior bombing campaign from 2015 onwards did not crush Houthi resolve, and the group has only grown stronger and more entrenched since then. The costs of renewed conflict would be substantial, and there is no indication a second attempt would succeed where the first failed.

The second option is diplomacy. But as Vivian Neerheim reports in the episode , the Houthis have a documented history of tabling maximalist demands during negotiations. They currently hold the upper hand—controlling the Bab al-Mandab Strait and other critical chokepoints—and feel emboldened by their military gains. Even if Saudi Arabia negotiates a settlement, there is no guarantee the agreement would be durable or that the Houthis would honor its terms.
"As long as there is still conflict in the region and as long as they have foes who are still willing and able to attack the pipeline, that will remain a risk."

f38107c05b.a: Saudi Arabia's entire economy and government budget depend on oil revenue, and their diversification efforts also rely on oil revenue to fund costly investments. f: Saudi Arabia's entire economy and government budget depend on oil revenue, and their diversification efforts also rely on oil sales to fund costly investments—meaning a sustained blockade of all export routes is an existential threat to the kingdom's stability . At the same time, Yemen is tilting back toward full-blown war, which threatens to devastate tens of millions already living in one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
An economy held hostage by blocked pipelines

Saudi Arabia has no real fallback plan if it cannot move oil to global markets. The kingdom's attempts to diversify—major investments in tourism, technology, and renewable energy—were all funded by oil revenue in the first place. As Vivian Neerheim explains in The Daily episode , blocking Saudi Arabia's oil exports is not simply an economic inconvenience; it strikes at the heart of how the kingdom finances everything. Without access to global markets, the government has no way to fund its ambitious Vision 2030 projects or sustain public spending .

The Houthis' control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and their demonstrated ability to strike at both the East-West Pipeline and shipping lanes in the Red Sea means Saudi Arabia faces a genuine dilemma. The kingdom cannot easily reopen these routes through negotiation—the Houthis remain hostile—and military solutions have already proven costly and ineffective in the past.
Yemen's slide into catastrophe

The humanitarian toll is equally stark. Yemen has been in crisis since the Houthis became a major power player in 2014 and Saudi Arabia launched its bombing campaign in 2015. A UN-backed truce signed in 2022 brought a fragile ceasefire, but the latest escalation is reversing that fragile peace and pushing the country back toward open conflict.
